sources.title: Recovered interview note containing the linked-list common-node prompt
Tagged repository question record for the first common linked-list node
Deterministic Java validation for all three requested algorithms

claims.text: The recovered source explicitly asks for the first common node of two linked lists and names three approaches: two-pointer switching, hashing, and length alignment; it does not specify cyclic-list handling.
The validated implementations and tests define a common node by object identity, including a negative case where equal node values belong to disjoint node objects.
The exact Java implementation contains the three requested strategies and the deterministic test executes all three against the same expected node identity.

The deterministic fixture covers null inputs, same-head intersection, a single shared tail node, unequal private-prefix lengths, equal-valued but disjoint nodes, and 3000 fixed-seed structures with independently retained expected shared-node references.

The candidate scopes the standard algorithms to acyclic singly linked lists and explicitly declines to claim direct correctness for cyclic inputs, because the recovered source does not state a cycle contract and the provided implementations are not cycle-aware.

checks: all three requested algorithms return the same expected node identity
equal node values without shared identity do not create a false intersection

boundary_tests.case: both lists are null or exactly one list is null
both heads are the same node object
boundary_tests.expected: the shared head is returned immediately as the first common node

boundary_tests.case: lists have unequal private prefixes followed by a retained shared tail
boundary_tests.expected: all three methods return the retained first shared-tail node identity

boundary_tests.case: two disjoint lists contain the same sequence of integer values
boundary_tests.expected: all three methods return null because equal values are not shared node identity

findings: The candidate answers exactly the three approaches named by the source instead of replacing the prompt with a generic linked-list template.
Object identity versus value equality is made explicit and is exercised by a dedicated disjoint equal-values test.
The two O(1)-space approaches are explained through path-length and distance-to-tail invariants rather than only presenting code.
Cycle handling is treated as an explicit out-of-scope boundary instead of silently claiming the acyclic algorithms handle cyclic inputs.
The deterministic fixture retains the expected shared node at construction time and tests 3000 fixed-seed structures, avoiding a circular oracle based on one of the three implementations.
No personal project results or production metrics are invented.
Required human approval remains a separate promotion gate and is not treated as satisfied by this automated isolated review.
